title: The Great Awokening started in 2014, not 2020
gist: Yglesias dates the Great Awokening to shifts visible around 2014, not the 2020 Covid/Floyd moment, using survey data on attributions of racial disparity; he credits the era with ending mainstream racial profiling but faults its thoughtless disparate-impact reasoning (e.g. anti-police arguments) and argues viral content distribution structurally entrenched sloppy thinking that persists.

insights.claim: The Great Awokening's underlying shifts were visible around 2014-2015, well before the 2020 Covid/George Floyd moment, even though the phenomenon reached its apogee 12 to 24 months after Yglesias's March 2019 Vox feature on it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes the timeline of the 'woke era,' which matters for anyone assessing how durable or cyclical the cultural-political shift is heading into 2028.
insights.quote: I wrote a big feature for Vox about what I called the Great Awokening back in March of 2019, which obviously was before Covid and before George Floyd.
insights.locator: The whole “Woke 1” discourse is a good joke

insights.claim: As recently as 2014 a majority of non-Black Democrats said 'no' when asked whether Black-white differences in jobs, income, and housing are mainly due to discrimination, then attributions to discrimination surged among non-Black Democrats and independents in the 2016, 2018, and 2022 surveys.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A single quantifiable indicator marking the attitude shift, useful for dating and measuring the cultural realignment rather than relying on vibes.
insights.quote: as recently as 2014, a majority of non-Black Democrats said “no” to this question
insights.locator: if you want a single clear data point

insights.claim: Support for willpower-based explanations of disparate racial outcomes collapsed, especially among Democrats, starting after 2012.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A second dated inflection reinforcing that the attitudinal shift predates 2020, sharpening the periodization of the Awokening.
insights.quote: support for that collapsed, especially among Democrats, starting after 2012
insights.locator: But it used to be that a majority of non-Black Americans

insights.claim: Yglesias's 2019 thinking was heavily shaped by William Julius Wilson's view that progress depended on winning political support for a race-neutral program of uplift for 'The Truly Disadvantaged.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Names the intellectual model behind class-first, race-neutral policy design — a framework re-emerging in post-woke Democratic strategy debates.
insights.quote: the big hope for progress in America was that we could secure political support for a race-neutral program of uplift for what he called The Truly Disadvantaged
insights.locator: If you want to understand how I was thinking about it in 2019

insights.claim: Late in life Martin Luther King Jr. framed his economic-uplift ideas as a program that would benefit all the poor, including the two-thirds who are white, and explicitly 'not a civil rights program' in the current sense.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Historical grounding for universalist, race-neutral policy framing as a coalition strategy rather than a retreat from racial justice.
insights.quote: would benefit all the poor, including the two-thirds of them who are white
insights.locator: Late in life, Martin Luther King Jr.

insights.claim: Right-wingers historically used divisive racial rhetoric to undermine white support for the social safety net, as when Rush Limbaugh branded the Affordable Care Act 'a civil rights bill' and 'reparations.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Identifies the racialization-of-welfare tactic as a recurring mode of American politics, relevant to how universal programs get attacked.
insights.quote: Rush Limbaugh would specifically describe the Affordable Care Act as “a civil rights bill” and “reparations”

insights.claim: Yglesias's optimistic read was that declining anti-Black sentiment among white Americans would undermine the right-wing style of racializing the safety net.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Frames falling racial resentment as a political enabler of universal social spending — a mechanism to watch as attitudes shift in the post-woke period.
insights.quote: declining anti-Black sentiment in the white population was going to undermine this style of right-wing politics
insights.locator: My optimistic read of the Great Awokening

themes.theme: Gains and excesses of the era

insights.claim: Overt advocacy for racial profiling as a law-enforcement strategy used to be fairly mainstream in American life, and a clear implication of the Great Awokening was to move away from that demeaning approach.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Credits the era with a genuine normative gain, complicating any wholesale dismissal of the period as purely excess.
insights.quote: overt advocacy for racial discrimination as a law enforcement strategy used to be pretty mainstream in American life
insights.locator: Now that we are in the post-woke era

insights.claim: The era also produced turbocharged, thoughtless disparate-impact analysis — most infamously the argument that because African Americans are disproportionately arrested, arresting people is racist and police should be abolished — with disastrous consequences for crime-prone Black neighborhoods.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A self-critical account of how a well-intentioned inference backfired on its intended beneficiaries, cautionary for evaluating impact-based policy arguments.
insights.quote: delivered a disproportionate negative impact on precisely the Black communities it was intended to help
insights.locator: But during “Woke 1” we also got a ton

insights.claim: A structural increase in sloppy thinking driven by viral content distribution is still with us even though the specific anti-police mode of thought has become unfashionable.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Attributes the deeper problem to the incentives of viral distribution rather than any one ideology, implying the failure mode recurs across future political fashions.
insights.quote: a structural increase in sloppy thinking due to viral content distribution is very much still with us
insights.locator: And, unfortunately, I think a structural increase

insights.claim: Pre-Awokening Democrats sounded markedly different, as when Obama in 2008 lectured Black audiences about personal responsibility and parenting — scolding parents for feeding kids 'cold Popeyes' and telling them not to 'just sit in the house watching SportsCenter.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of how far Democratic racial rhetoric shifted, a baseline for gauging any post-woke reversion.
insights.quote: here’s Obama at a Black church in 2008 talking about how fathers are “missing from too many lives and too many homes,”
insights.locator: Incidentally, for the young people out there

insights.claim: Obama's personal-responsibility rhetoric was a frequent point of contention with progressive African American intellectuals like Ta-Nehisi Coates, and he shifted away from it in his second term as the Awokening gathered steam.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Ties an elite intellectual conflict to a datable shift in a president's messaging, illustrating how the Awokening reshaped Democratic discourse from within.
insights.quote: Ta-Nehisi Coates really didn’t like it and Nia-Malika Henderson wrote an insightful piece about Obama shifting away from it in his second term
insights.locator: This was a frequent bone of contention

insights.claim: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' is a huge hit with a decent chance of becoming the top-grossing film of all time in nominal terms, yet its broadly-appealing, unremarkable 'going to the movies' quality is exactly what post-pandemic streaming and short-form culture has eroded.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A read on the collapse of the mass moviegoing habit and the survival of only tentpole monoculture events — relevant to theatrical-exhibition and studio-slate economics.
insights.quote: isn’t this sort of “Hey, let’s go to the movies!” vibe exactly what’s gone away in post-pandemic America, with its endless streaming and short-form options?
